title: Port Development Bonds

narrative.text: Elara Vostane has called you to the Finance Ministry for what she describes as a 'routine fiscal matter.' When Elara describes something as routine, it is almost never routine. She is waiting in her office with a prospectus for the Aldenmoor Port Development Bonds — a government-issued infrastructure bond that finances the expansion of the Amber Coast's primary deep-water port. The bonds pay 4% annually and mature in three years. She is offering you a personal allocation: 2,000 VK in bonds at the institutional rate.

Before you ask — yes, this is legal. The bonds are publicly listed. Any Veltrian citizen can purchase them. What makes this allocation different is the rate: institutional investors get a preferential yield that retail investors do not. As Chancellor, you qualify as an institutional investor under the Treasury's definition. The return is modest — 2,000 VK becomes approximately 4,000 by Week 40. It is safe, boring, and exactly the kind of investment a prudent person makes. I am telling you about it because it is my job to ensure you are aware of your financial options. Not every investment is a scandal waiting to happen. Some are just bonds.

Safe. Boring. Legal. Elara is telling me the truth — these bonds are publicly available and the institutional rate is a standard Treasury practice. But there is something she has not mentioned: the Free Trade Zone Act. It is being drafted now and will reach parliament in a few months. If it passes, the Aldenmoor port becomes the center of a free trade zone, and the bonds' value will more than double. I will be the one who signs or vetoes that act. If I invest now and sign later, that 4,000 VK return will look very different in retrospect. Elara knows this. She is testing whether I see the conflict — or whether I am the kind of person who pretends not to see it.

monologue: The bonds are legal. Elara has made that clear. What she has not made clear — what she wants me to notice without her having to say it — is the Free Trade Zone Act. If I invest now and sign later, the institutional rate becomes a conflict-of-interest headline. She is offering me a test disguised as a financial opportunity. I am supposed to notice the test.

choices.text: "I will take the allocation, Elara. Thank you for bringing it to my attention. These are government bonds — publicly listed, legally issued, available to any institutional investor. I am an institutional investor. If the Free Trade Zone Act passes and increases the value of the bonds, that is a consequence of good policy, not corruption. I will not avoid making the right decision for the country because it might also benefit my personal finances. That is not ethics — it is timidity. Make the allocation."

reactions.text: She writes the allocation on her pad — 2,000 VK, institutional rate. She does not comment. The silence is the sound of Elara Vostane executing an instruction and filing the ethical concern for later.

choices.text: "No, Elara. I know they are legal. I know any citizen can buy them. But I am not 'any citizen' — I am the person who will decide whether the Free Trade Zone Act becomes law. If I invest in port bonds now and sign that act later, every journalist in Veltria will be able to draw a line between those two facts. That line will be fair. It will be accurate. And it will make me look like exactly the kind of politician I campaigned against. Find me an investment that has no connection to government policy — a diversified fund, an international bond, something genuinely at arm's length. I will invest in that. I will not invest in this."

reactions.text: She writes find arm's-length investment on her pad and makes a note to contact the Treasury. She does not argue. She presented the option — you declined it. The matter is closed.

choices.text: "Buy the bonds — but put them in a blind trust. I want a legal instrument that prevents me from knowing the specific contents of my portfolio. The trust manager makes investment decisions independently. I make policy decisions independently. Neither of us knows what the other is doing. If the Free Trade Zone Act passes and the bonds appreciate, I will not know whether I own them — and even if I suspect, I will have no ability to act on that suspicion. This is how it works in mature democracies, Elara. We should act like one."

reactions.text: She writes blind trust on her pad. She did not anticipate this solution — you can tell by the slight pause before the pen moves. It is not often that Elara Vostane encounters a solution she did not anticipate.
